title: Robust Ion-Photon Entanglement via Polarization-to-Time-Bin Conversion
authors: Ana Luiza Ferrari, Denton Wu, Mika A. Zalewski, Norbert M. Linke
abstract: Time-bin photonic qubits are well-suited for quantum network applications due to their robustness to polarization instability in fiber links and potential for heterogeneous networks. In this work, we implement the first entanglement-preserving polarization-to-time-bin conversion of a photon qubit in an entangled state with a matter qubit. Photons initially generated with polarization encoding are converted to the time-bin basis through a polarization-discriminating asymmetric Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The photonic qubits are generated via the $1092$ nm transition of a $^{88}$Sr$^{+}$ ion. We measure state fidelity bounds of $0.906 \pm 0.011 \le \mathcal{F} \le 0.934\pm 0.011$, with conversion error $< 0.028$, and find this fidelity is unaffected by depolarizing noise even at full depolarization strength.
summary: The research demonstrates an entanglement-preserving method to convert photonic qubits from polarization encoding to the more stable time-bin basis using trapped ${}^{88}	ext{Sr}^+$ ions. By implementing this conversion, the authors show that the resulting entangled state fidelity remains high and is robust against significant depolarizing noise, which is crucial for practical quantum communication networks.
main_problem: The primary challenge is overcoming polarization instability inherent in quantum communication links when distributing entanglement between matter qubits (trapped ions) and photons.
main_result: The implementation of a polarization-to-time-bin conversion successfully preserves entanglement fidelity, proving robust against depolarizing noise even at full depolarization strength.
method: The authors use an asymmetric Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) as an encoder to convert the initial polarization encoding into a time-bin basis for the photonic qubit.
model_or_system: The system involves trapped ${}^{88}	ext{Sr}^+$ ions acting as matter qubits, emitting photons at $1092 	ext{ nm}$. The process requires two interferometers (encoder and decoder) to map polarization states ($|Hangle, |Vangle$) onto time-bins ($|Eangle, |Langle$).
key_observables: State fidelity bounds ($\approx 0.91 - 0.93$), conversion error ($< 0.028$), and the robustness of fidelity against depolarizing noise.
important_parameters: Time-bin separation (60 ns), ion transition wavelength (1092 nm), and depolarization strength parameter ($p$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that background counts are negligible for post-selected fidelity, and the phase error estimation is a conservative upper bound due to shared common-mode drift.
figures_summary: Figures detail the MZI encoder/decoder setups (Fig. 1), show population measurements and coherence fringes for time-bin encoding (Fig. 2), illustrate the phase stabilization scheme (Fig. 4, Fig. 5), and compare fidelity vs. noise strength for both encoding methods (Fig. 3).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the need for robust entanglement distribution, detailing the physical implementation of the polarization-to-time-bin conversion using MZIs, quantifying the resulting state fidelity and error sources through detailed measurements, and finally demonstrating the superior noise resilience of the time-bin encoding.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical bottleneck in quantum networking—maintaining coherence over long distances where fiber polarization drift is common. The successful demonstration of robust entanglement transfer via time-bin encoding is highly relevant to building scalable quantum repeaters and networks.

FIG. 2. Fidelity of the time-bin encoded ion-photon entangled state. (a) Populations of the time-bin encoded ion-photon state. Each column shows a measured diagonal term of the density matrix. The black boxes indicate the ideal popula- tions. (b) Diagonal basis correlations of the time-bin encoded ion-photon state. When the photons are in an early/late su- perposition, the probability of measuring a bright ion changes sinusoidally as a function of the phase of the ion analy- sis pulse. The dashed lines show the theoretical amplitude given our unbalanced ion-photon state. From (a) and (b), we calculate bounds on the converted ion-photon fidelity of 0.906 ± 0.011 ≤F ≤0.934 ± 0.011.

FIG. 3. Fidelity bounds for the polarization (a) and time-bin (b) encoded ion-photon state as a function of the depolarizing strength p. While the polarization-encoded ion-photon state fidelity degrades as a function of p, the time-bin state fidelity remains unaffected. Data at p = 0 and p = 1 are measured with the depolarizing channel off and on, respectively; intermediate points are statistical mixtures of the two datasets with weight p. Inset: Stokes parameters measured at the output of the fiber squeezer given a horizontally polarized input laser, recorded for one minute, showing depolarization at p = 1. Each point in (a) and (b) takes over one minute to acquire.

Fig. 5 shows the phase stabilization performance of each board during 500 s on the photon path. When no correction is applied, the phase undergoes uncontrolled drift. The 1033 nm lock suppresses oscillations but has a slow monotonic drift. By recentering the interferom- eter fringe every 10 s, this drift is suppressed. In the experiment, we conservatively recenter once per 30 s and observe no fidelity improvement from a higher recenter- ing frequency. We attribute the tolerance to infrequent recentering to the largely common-mode drift between the two boards, which sit next to each other on the same optical table.
